APPROACH TO JAUNDICE 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If unstable first resuscitate: 
ABCs, IV, monitors, check glucose, pregnancy 
test in appropriate female patients 
HISTORY AND EXAMINATION 
 
Ask about pain, fever, prior surgeries, time of onset, medications, herbal medications, 
alcohol/drug use, HIV history, travel, work, and family history. 
 
Exam must include vital signs (fever/hypotension – consider cholangitis), mental status, 
neurologic exam, presence of asterixis, lungs (crackles, pleural effusions), CVS (evidence of 
heart failure), abdomen: presence of ascites, tenderness, masses, hepatosplenomegaly, 
and skin (spider naevi, ecchymoses, dilated abdominal wall vessels) 
 
INITIAL INVESTIGATIONS 
 
Laboratory tests: FBC/U&E/complete LFT/LDH/CMP/CRP/lipase/INR/VBG and 
glucose/paracetamol level if suspected overdose 
If viral hepatitis suspected: HepA IgM/HepB SAg/HepB cAb/HepC Ab 
Travel history to endemic region: malaria rapid and smear 
Initial imaging: CXR/POCUS 
Other: ECG/ urine dipstick and bHCG 
Subsequent imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: assess biliary system, hepatic 
architecture and vessels, presence of any masses 
MANAGEMENT OF ACUTE LIVER FAILURE 
(see acute liver failure protocol) 
 
NB. Treat the cause 
 
If decompensated liver failure in patient with cirrhosis: search for and correct precipitants: 
GI bleed, infection, uraemia, electrolyte abnormalities, drugs/toxins, ↑ protein in diet or 
non-adherence to treatment  
Supportive care: 
§ 
Correct electrolyte abnormalities: esp. ↑/↓ Na+, ↓K+ and ↓ Mg2+ 
§ 
Monitor and correct hypoglycaemia 
§ 
Monitor fluid status: diuretics if overloaded 
§ 
Correct coagulopathy: if bleeding consider Vit K 5-10mg SC and FFPs 
§ 
For GI bleeding: transfuse blood products, IV PPI, consider somatostatin and 
urgent surgical referral (refer to protocol) 
§ 
Monitor GCS: if prolonged history of confusion or focal signs (including seizures) 
– urgent CTB to exclude ICH 
§ 
For raised ICP may require mannitol 0.5-1g/kg IV bolus 
WEST HAVEN GRADING HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY 
 
Grade 0: 
minimal/subclinical 
No clinical manifestations, some abnormalities on 
psychometric testing 
Grade I: mild 
Euphoria/depression, mild confusion, slurred speech, 
disordered sleep, asterixis may/may not be present 
Grade II: moderate 
Lethargy, moderate confusion, asterixis usually present 
Grade III: severe 
Marked confusion, incoherent speech, drowsy but rousable, 
asterixis present 
Grade IV: coma 
Comatose 
CAUSES FULMINANT HEPATIC FAILURE 
 
A 
Acetaminophen (paracetamol), Hep A, autoimmune hepatitis 
B 
Hep B, Budd-Chiari syndrome 
C 
Hep C, CMV, cryptogenic 
D 
Hep D, drugs/toxins – mushroom ingestion (Amanita), herbal ingestion 
E 
Extra causes: Wilson’s disease 
F 
Fatty infiltration: acute fatty liver of pregnancy, Reye’s syndrome 
REFERENCES 
Gareth Roberts, "Decompensated Liver Disease and what we can do about it in the ED. St Emlyns," in St.Emlyn's, September 12
